chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
title: How King Oliver played
summary: Reason describes Oliver's endurance, mouthpiece practice, rhythm choruses and breathing technique.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Did he have trouble with his lip much in those times?
Not too much. Used to, uh, you'd see him sitting in the bus all the time. He'd, he'd, he'd kept his lip up, you know, in the daytime. Hard trumpet players do.
Using his mouthpiece or just his hands? Just his mouthpiece. Mm-hmm. He used it. Well, how long, how many choruses could he play at that time?
As long as a band could stand up under him.
Oh, so he was still going?

Well, at during that time, we weren't doing the things that he did when Paul was with the band. Yeah. See, he weren't playing those, those kind of, those arrangements like that, see. Mm-hmm. And, uh, but I mean during the time when, when I was with him, when I first joined him, he could take 50 or 100 chords and think nothing else. And neither one of them was just alike. Oh, gee. He knew how to balance, just take a little bit off, a little bit off, tape off, tape off, tape off. Mm-hmm. And, and the way he used to do, he used to sit right next to the piano. And, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the reed section would take two rhythm choruses and he would play the rhythm underneath him. Then the brass section would play the rhythm underneath him. Then the rhythm section would play two choruses. And he would make that rhyme on him just like that. Mm-hmm. And he'd be playing that top solo all the time. Mm-hmm. And it's, it's a pity that in those days we didn't have these tape recorders like we have now.

And, uh, and one of the things that he told me, and I'm sorry that we never did get a chance to do it, as he told me he had another composition that he, uh, wanted to write, that he had in mind and he wanted me to write it for him. But we.

never did he get a chance to get around to doing it. But so far as for playing these many choruses, it wasn't the idea of an exceptional amount of power, it was technique. Kings never get sold. They never get sold. But he knew just how much to put in and how to take advantage of everything. He knew how to breathe, he taught Louie that. He could breathe in and out. While he was playing he could breathe in and out. And he could hold a note and breathe while he was holding it. You couldn't tell the difference. And he could hold that horn away from his lip just like that. And it was a big high note. And you say you knew how to taper off? Oh yeah. Now you mean by that? Not taper off, take off. Oh, take off. From one chorus. How to progress one chorus, you see. And to the next chorus. And they were both. You knew it was King Oliver, but they
